summary: Gives a corrected description of the control commands exchanged between Network Control Programs to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol of RFC 123. It fixes an error in RFC 127 pointed out by Eric Harslem of Rand. It was replaced by RFC 165.

eli5.summary: A corrected script for the opening steps of a call between computers. An earlier version had a mistake, and this one fixes it.

subtitle: A corrected listing of the control commands that two NCPs exchange to run the Initial Connection Protocol.

tldr.problem: The earlier description of the control commands behind the Initial Connection Protocol of RFC 123 contained an error, found by Eric Harslem of RAND.
tldr.mechanism: A table lists, side by side, what the server NCP and the user NCP send: RTS, STR, ALL and CLS commands with sockets and links, ending with a second connection on which data flows.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 127 and was itself later obsoleted by RFC 165.

facts.label: Initial data
facts.value: 32 bits in 1 message on link l_A

today: RFC 145 is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 165 and updated by RFC 143. It obsoleted RFC 127.

sections.title: What This Note Gives
sections.content: The author offers his interpretation of the exchange between Network Control Programs (NCPs) that is needed to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol of RFC 123. The note corrects an error pointed out by Eric Harslem of RAND, and it obsoletes RFC 127.
sections.eli5: It is the fixed version of a recipe for how two computers say hello and set up a conversation.

sections.title: The Command Exchange
sections.content:
The server NCP listens for a connection on socket L. The user NCP sends RTS, U, L, l_A. The server answers with STR, L, U, 32 and the user side with ALL, l_A, 1, 32. The server then sends 32 bits of data in one message on link l_A. Its value is S.

Both sides then send CLS to close the first connection. They go on to open new connections using that value: STR, S+1, U+1, B_s on the server side and STR, U+1, S, B_u on the user side, plus RTS, S, U+1, l_B and RTS, U, S+1, l_C. Each waits for its connection, then allocates messages and bits with ALL, and data flows between the links l_B and l_C.
sections.eli5: First the computers use one phone line only to swap a secret number. Then they hang up and call back on new lines picked using that number, and talk for real.

sections.title: Notation
sections.content: In the table, l_A, l_B and l_C are links, m_B and m_C are message allocations, and b_B and b_C are bit allocations. All other symbols are defined in RFC 123. The command names are RTS, STR, ALL and CLS.
sections.eli5: The little letters are just names for the lines and the amounts of data allowed, like labels on boxes.
